newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: ALLEGED PORT ARTHUR GUNMAN FACES COURT
Alleged Port Arthur Gunman, Martin Bryant, will appear in Hobart's Supreme Court this morning to face 70 charges, including 35 of murder.
It's been five months since 35 people were shot dead, and another 19 wounded at the Port Arthur penal colony site in Tasmania's south.
The incident has been described as the world's worst massacre by a lone gunman.
Since then, more than 15-hundred people have received counselling by the Port Arthur Recovery Team's counselling corps, and the State's tourism industry has faced a massive downturn.
If Martin Bryant pleads guilty this morning, the court is likely to adjourn until Thursday with a sentence expected on Friday.
If he pleads not guilty, the trial's scheduled to start in Mid November.
HILL SAYS REASONS TO BE OUTLINED SOON

Federal Environment Minister, Robert Hill, says the Government put in considerable effort to ensure the Port Hinchinbrook development, near Cardwell in north Queensland, will not detrimentally effect World Heritage values.
Senator Hill says the reasons for approving Keith William's project will be released within days.
Senator Robert Hill was responding to a call from conservationists to release the reasons, so they can mount a legal challenge to his decision.
MESSAGES FLOOD INTO MARGARET RIVER
The town of Margaret River has been flooded with messages of sympathy from around Australia following the deaths of nine people in a rock fall.
Among those expressing sympathy are the Army chaplains from Townsville in Queensland, where 18 soldiers died during a training exercise earlier this year.
The names of the victims, five adults and four primary school children were read out during a service at Margaret River's Saint Thomas Moore Catholic Church yesterday.
Father Pat Rooney asked the congregation to pray for families of the victims and the emergency service personnel suffering trauma after pulling the bodies from the rubble.
HERRON UP NORTH THIS WEEK
The Northern Territory ATSIC Manager says some Aboriginal organisations are still angry over Federal Government funding cuts.
They'll have a chance to voice their concerns to Aboriginal Affairs Minister John Herron, when he starts a week-long visit to the Territory in Darwin today.
Senator Herron will also visit the Nhulunbuy, Tennant Creek and Papunya regions.
Mr Kelly says the main purpose of the visit is for the Minister to get a better appreciation for the specific concerns or problems and service delivery difficulties experienced in the Territory.
He says Aboriginal service organisations have a lot to gain from the visit.
CARR INSISTS ICAC IS ACCOUNTABLE
The New South Wales Premier says there's no accountability problem in the state's Independent Commission Against Corruption, because it answers to a Parliamentary Committee.
Bob Carr's comments follow the agreement by State and Territory leaders to review the accountability and efficiency of investigatory bodies.
At last week's the leaders meeting, Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett said ICAC should be wound up because it wasn't accountable.
But Mr Carr says Mr Kennett's concerns are unwaranted because the Parliamentary Committee oversees ICAC's operations.
SUSPECT IN 10-YEAR-OLD DISAPPEARANCE
In Sydney, Bondi police say they have a have a suspect in a ten year-old child disappearance case.
Nine-year-old Samantha Knight disappeared without a trace in a Bondi Street on August the 19th, 1986.
Detective Senior constable David Donahue says police have fresh information about the case after interviewing a man in July who is now considered a suspect.
The man is known to the young girls' mother Tess Knight, but she says his significance in the disappearance didn't strike her when Sam went missing.
PUBLIC LOSING WITH COMMUNITY BASED ORGANISATION-STUDY
A new national study into how governments are treating their community-based government funded organisations, suggests the public is losing out.
The study shows there are some services that can't be treated like a business.
Associate professor Mark Lyons from the University of technology in Sydney, says some disturbing results have come through.
Associate Professor Lyons says the personal impact of service cuts are being ignored.
He says of all the states and territories, South Australia is doing the best, as its approach is more of a partnership model.
NEWMAN TO BE INVITED TO ADDRESS RALLY
The Community and Public Sector Union will invite Tasmania's senior Federal minister, Jocelyn Newman, to address a rally in Launceston today protesting against Federal budget cuts.
Social Security Minister, Senator Newman, will open new departmental offices and a family service centre in Charles Street.
At the same time, community groups, tertiary students and the CPSU will be rallying at the Civic Square.
The State secretary of the CPSU, Matthew Reynolds, says the aim is to make Senator Newman more accountable for her role in the budget cuts.
HEROES WELCOME FOR MANLY
A 10-minute long deafening cheer last night welcomed home this year's rugby league premiers at the Manly leagues club at Brookvale.
About seven thousand cheering supporters gathered at the club to celebrate yesterday's 20 points to 8 win over St George at the Sydney football stadium.
Adding to the team's glory, Manly captain Geoff Toovey won the Churchill Medal for the best player on ground.
And six Manly players were named in the Australian squad to play in the upcoming tour of Papua New Guinea.
